description: Test your knowledge of PA H4 | Macrocytic Anemias & B12/Folate.

cards.text: Describe the 5-step pathway for vitamin B12 absorption from food to portal blood.
cards.answer: 1) Gastric acid releases protein-bound B12; 2) Salivary haptocorrin (R-protein) binds free B12; 3) Pancreatic proteases transfer B12 from R-protein to intrinsic factor (IF) in duodenum; 4) Parietal cells secrete IF which binds B12 protectively; 5) IF-B12 binds cubilin-AMN receptors in terminal ileum and enters portal blood bound to transcobalamin II.

tip.tip: RIF pathway: R-protein → Intrinsic Factor → Terminal ileum Receptor

cards.text: Where is intrinsic factor produced and what happens if it is deficient?
cards.answer: Intrinsic factor is secreted by gastric parietal cells of the fundus and body. Without IF, B12 cannot bind the cubilin receptor in the terminal ileum and is lost in feces, causing pernicious anemia even with normal dietary B12 intake.

tip.tip: Parietal cells = IF factory. No parietal cells (autoimmune or post-gastrectomy) = no B12 absorption

cards.text: Why does vitamin B12 deficiency develop slowly (3–5 years) after dietary omission, but folate deficiency develops rapidly (3–4 months)?
cards.answer: B12 hepatic stores (3–5 mg) are vast, but more importantly the body recycles B12 via enterohepatic circulation (bile → terminal ileum reabsorption). Folate stores (3–4 mg) lack this recycling mechanism, so daily losses deplete stores within months.

tip.tip: B12 recycled = slow loss. Folate no recycling = fast loss. Same amount stored, but different fates.

cards.text: Compare the anatomical sites of absorption for vitamin B12 versus folate. What is the clinical significance?
cards.answer: B12 is absorbed exclusively in the terminal ileum (~100 cm) via cubilin receptors. Folate is absorbed throughout the proximal jejunum via reduced folate carrier. Consequently, terminal ileal disease or resection causes B12 deficiency but spares folate; proximal jejunal disease causes folate deficiency but spares B12.

tip.tip: B12 = Bottom (terminal ileum); Folate = Front (proximal jejunum)

cards.text: Name the two enzymes in human cells that require vitamin B12 as a cofactor and describe their key functions.
cards.answer: 1) Methionine synthase: 5-methyl-THF + homocysteine → THF + methionine (produces SAM for myelin and methylation). 2) Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase: methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA (propionate metabolism). Only these two reactions depend on B12 in humans.

tip.tip: MS = Methyl synthesis (SAM ← methionine). MUT = Methylmalonic catabolism.

cards.text: What is the 'folate trap' and why does it occur in B12 deficiency?
cards.answer: Methionine synthase (B12-dependent) converts 5-methyl-THF to THF. Without B12, 5-methyl-THF accumulates and cannot donate its methyl group, trapping folate in an unusable form. This causes functional folate deficiency despite normal or elevated serum folate levels.

tip.tip: B12 ↓ → 5-methyl-THF stuck → folate 'locked' → macrocytosis despite high folate blood levels

cards.text: What is the metabolic consequence of impaired methionine synthase activity in B12 deficiency?
cards.answer: Homocysteine accumulates because it cannot be converted to methionine by methionine synthase. Elevated homocysteine is toxic to vascular endothelium, causes thrombosis, and contributes to the vascular and neurological complications (subacute combined degeneration) of B12 deficiency.

cards.text: Why does B12 deficiency but not folate deficiency cause subacute combined degeneration (SCD) of the spinal cord?
cards.answer: B12 is required for myelin synthesis via SAM production (methionine synthase pathway) and energy production in neurons (methylmalonic-CoA mutase pathway). B12 deficiency causes both demyelination and mitochondrial dysfunction in long spinal cord tracts. Folate deficiency does not directly impair these pathways and causes only macrocytic anemia without neurological symptoms.

tip.tip: B12 = myelin + neurons. Folate = DNA synthesis only. No B12 → spinal cord dies.
